passage: At break time in their Kolkata school, Nikita, a bigger girl from the next class, snatched Zubin's toy tractor. "Give it or I'll push you," she hissed. Zubin froze. His eyes filled and he let go without a word. Later Miss Anjali noticed him hunched on the bench and asked what happened. He whispered it. She knelt beside him. "Thank you for telling me. It's not your fault." She went to find Nikita at once and got the tractor back. Then she practised with him: "Stand tall, say STOP loudly, then come to me." Zubin tried. "STOP!" It came out bigger than he expected.

qa.q: What did Nikita snatch from Zubin?
qa.a: Nikita snatched Zubin's toy tractor.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he froze and let go?
qa.a: Zubin felt frightened by Nikita's threat to push him, so he froze and gave up the tractor without a word.

qa.q: How did Miss Anjali help Zubin, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She thanked him, said it was not his fault, dealt with Nikita straight away and practised a loud "STOP", so Zubin learned that telling works.

qa.q: How might Nikita see it when Miss Anjali comes to find her?
qa.a: Nikita may feel caught and a bit worried, and learn that grabbing and threats get noticed by adults.

grounding: Illustrates a child freezing and giving up a toy to a bully, then learning to say stop loudly and tell the teacher.

passage:
"That's my bucket. Give it."
"N-no, I'm using it."
"Give it, or you can't come to the sandpit again."
Jyoti's hands went stiff. She pushed the bucket across and started to cry.
"Jyoti, what happened?" Afreen Ma'am had seen from the swings.
"Nothing."
"You look scared. You can tell me."
"Rohan took my bucket. He said I can't come back."
"Thank you for telling me. That wasn't fair, and it's not your fault. Let's sort it out right now." Afreen Ma'am walked over with her, and Rohan handed the bucket back.
"Next time, shout STOP like a lion, then come to me. Try it."
"STOP!"
"Brilliant."

qa.q: What did Rohan say Jyoti couldn't do?
qa.a: Rohan said Jyoti can't come to the sandpit again.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti first answer "Nothing"?
qa.a: Jyoti was scared of Rohan's threat and perhaps worried that telling would make things worse, so she hid it at first.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do next time someone grabs her things?
qa.a: Shout "STOP" like a lion and then go straight to Afreen Ma'am, as they practised.

qa.q: How does Afreen Ma'am see Jyoti's stiff hands and tears?
qa.a: Afreen Ma'am reads them as signs of fear and gently invites Jyoti to talk, instead of accepting "Nothing."

grounding: Shows a child crying and handing over a toy to a bully, then telling a teacher and practising a loud "stop".

passage: Annual Day was two hours away and the hall was a riot of drums and costumes. During the last rehearsal, Sarika kept poking the girl beside her with her paper wand. Raghav Sir crouched to her level, speaking under the noise. "Sarika, poking hurts, even with paper. Keep the wand up here, like a star." Sarika's cheeks went pink. She turned to the girl. "Sorry, Tanya." When the music started again, she held the wand high and steady. At the end Raghav Sir gave her a thumbs-up, and she grinned all the way to the dressing room.

qa.q: How long was it until Annual Day?
qa.a: Annual Day was two hours away.

qa.q: Why did Sarika's cheeks go pink when Raghav Sir spoke to her?
qa.a: Sarika felt a little embarrassed at being corrected, but his calm, kind words showed he cared, so she said sorry.

qa.q: Which choice by Raghav Sir worked, and why?
qa.a: He crouched to her level, explained that poking hurts and showed what to do instead, so the correction felt like help, not rejection.

qa.q: How might Tanya see Sarika's apology?
qa.a: Tanya probably feels relieved and a bit happier, since the poking stopped and Sarika said sorry herself.

grounding: Illustrates a child listening to a teacher's correction, saying sorry and trying again, feeling the correction as care.

passage: In the art room of a Chandigarh school, Payal scribbled a big black line across Meher's sunflower because Meher had taken the yellow crayon. Meher burst into tears. Baljeet Ma'am came over and knelt. "Payal, I can see you wanted the yellow. Scribbling on Meher's work isn't okay. How can we help her?" Payal stared at her shoes, then looked up. "Sorry, Meher. I'll help fix it." Together they turned the black line into a stem. When Baljeet Ma'am patted her shoulder, Payal leaned into her side for a moment.

qa.q: Why did Payal scribble on Meher's sunflower?
qa.a: Because Meher had taken the yellow crayon.

qa.q: Why did Payal lean into Baljeet Ma'am's side at the end?
qa.a: Payal felt comforted and cared for, not rejected, after being corrected kindly, and trusted her teacher.

qa.q: How could a teacher keep correction feeling like care?
qa.a: Name what the child wanted, say clearly what isn't okay, and invite them to fix it, as Baljeet Ma'am did.

qa.q: How does Meher see Payal helping turn the line into a stem?
qa.a: Meher likely feels her hurt was taken seriously and is pleased her sunflower got fixed.

grounding: Shows a child accepting a teacher's correction, apologising and repairing the harm, with the correction felt as care.

passage:
Monday: Asif knocked over the paint water. Deepak Sir shouted in front of everyone, "Careless! Always making a mess!" Asif stared at the floor and didn't say a word for the rest of the class.
Wednesday: Asif snapped a borrowed crayon. He glanced at Deepak Sir's desk, then slid the pieces under the cupboard.
Friday: Asif tore his worksheet while rubbing out a mistake. He crumpled it into his bag and sat with empty hands. When Deepak Sir asked where his sheet was, Asif just shook his head, eyes on his knees.

qa.q: Where did Asif slide the broken crayon pieces?
qa.a: Asif slid the pieces under the cupboard.

qa.q: Why did Asif hide the crayon and the torn worksheet?
qa.a: Asif was afraid of being shouted at again, so he hid his mistakes instead of telling Deepak Sir.

qa.q: What could Deepak Sir try instead of shouting?
qa.a: Calmly say "Oops, let's get a cloth" and show Asif how to fix a spill, so mistakes feel safe to own.

qa.q: How might Deepak Sir see Asif's silence on Friday?
qa.a: Deepak Sir may read it as stubbornness, not seeing that his own shouting taught Asif to hide.

grounding: Illustrates a child going silent and avoiding eye contact after harsh correction, and learning to hide mistakes instead of fixing them.

passage: The inspector was due at eleven, the fans had stopped in a power cut, and Ayesha Miss was rushing through number work. When Keerthana wrote a 6 backwards on the board, Ayesha Miss snapped, "Wrong again! Sit down." The class giggled. Keerthana walked back with her head down and didn't look up once. Later, stuck on a sum, she didn't raise her hand. She rubbed out her answer until the paper went thin, then hid the page under her lunch box. At home time Ayesha Miss found it and sighed. "Keerthana, I was too sharp today. Shall we fix this one together tomorrow?"

qa.q: When was the inspector due?
qa.a: The inspector was due at eleven.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana hide the page under her lunch box?
qa.a: Keerthana felt afraid and ashamed after being snapped at in front of the class, so she hid her mistake instead of asking for help.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Rushed, sharp words taught Keerthana to hide mistakes; a calm apology and fixing sums together, as Ayesha Miss offered, can rebuild trust.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha Miss when she finds the thin, rubbed-out page?
qa.a: Ayesha Miss probably feels regret, seeing how her sharp words made Keerthana too scared to ask.

grounding: Shows how harsh correction under pressure makes a child go silent and hide a mistake instead of fixing it.

passage: At the kindergarten in Buenos Aires, the tidy-up bell rang. Rania crossed her arms and turned her back on the block tower. "No. I'm not tidying." Valentina, her teacher, didn't raise her voice or call her naughty. She crouched nearby. "Blocks go in the box before snack. That's our rule every day. I'll put the first one in with you." Rania stamped. "No!" Valentina waited, humming the tidy-up song, while the others lined up. After a minute Rania dropped one block in, then another, scowling. "Thank you. Now snack," said Valentina, as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: What did Valentina offer to do with Rania?
qa.a: Valentina offered to put the first block in the box with her.

qa.q: What was Rania feeling when she crossed her arms and said "No"?
qa.a: Rania felt stubborn and cross about ending play, and was testing whether the tidy-up rule really held.

qa.q: Which choice by Valentina worked, and why?
qa.a: Valentina stayed calm, repeated the everyday rule without shaming, and waited, so Rania had nothing to fight against and tidied.

qa.q: How might Valentina see Rania's "No!"?
qa.a: Valentina seems to see it as ordinary limit-testing for a young child, not rudeness, so she stays patient.

grounding: Illustrates a child refusing a teacher's instruction and a calm, firm routine working better than shame.

passage: At the daycare in Bhopal, lunch meant washing hands first. Yamini turned her face to the wall. "No! Not washing." The helper aunty clicked her tongue. "Chhee, dirty girl! Everyone will laugh." Yamini's lip stuck out further, and she sat down on the floor. Alka Ma'am knelt beside her. "Hands get washed before lunch, every day. Do you want the blue soap or the green?" Yamini peeked. "Green." "Green it is." Alka Ma'am held out her hand and waited. Yamini got up, still pouting, and walked to the basin.

qa.q: Which soap did Yamini choose?
qa.a: Yamini chose the green soap.

qa.q: Why did Yamini sit on the floor after the helper aunty spoke?
qa.a: Yamini felt ashamed and angry at being called dirty, so she dug in harder instead of washing.

qa.q: Why did Alka Ma'am's approach work better than the helper aunty's?
qa.a: Alka Ma'am kept the rule calm and firm and offered a small choice, while shaming only made Yamini resist more.

qa.q: How might the helper aunty see Alka Ma'am's calm success?
qa.a: The helper aunty might feel surprised, and could learn that a small choice works better than scolding.

grounding: Shows a child refusing and turning away, with shaming making it worse and a calm, firm routine with a choice ending it.

passage: Dark clouds rolled over the colony park. "Gautam, home now. It's going to pour," Papa called. Gautam hung off the slide. "Just five minutes, Papa! I'll be good all evening!" Papa glanced at the sky. "Not today. When the weather's fine, you get your five-minute warning, like always." Gautam's big brother Mohit laughed. "He always does the warning. It's true." Gautam slid down once more, grumbling, and ran. The next evening, the sky was clear. "Five more minutes?" Gautam asked. "Deal," said Papa, and when the time was up, Gautam came without a fuss.

qa.q: Who said Papa always does the warning?
qa.a: Gautam's big brother Mohit said it.

qa.q: Why did Gautam come without a fuss the next evening?
qa.a: Gautam felt he could trust Papa's deals, since Papa had been fair and kept his word, so he was content to keep his side.

qa.q: What makes Papa's approach to bargaining fair?
qa.a: Papa says no clearly when there is a real reason, like the storm, and says yes to fair deals when he can, always keeping the same warning rule.

qa.q: How does Papa see Gautam's "I'll be good all evening"?
qa.a: Papa sees it as a bargain he can't accept with rain coming, but he respects that Gautam is trying to negotiate.

grounding: Illustrates a child bargaining with "just five minutes" and learning that deals work with a parent who is fair and consistent.

passage: At bedtime in their Bengaluru flat, Pankaj clutched the tablet. "Just five minutes, Mummy! I'll be good, I'll brush fast!" Yesterday Minakshi, his mother, had said no three times and then given in when he cried, and now he was already winding up to cry. She sat beside him. "I said yes yesterday because you cried. That made the rule wobbly, and that wasn't fair to you. Screen time ends at eight. After brushing you can choose one story or two songs." Pankaj wailed for a while. Minakshi stayed calm and kept the same rule. He brushed, and chose two songs.

qa.q: What time does screen time end in Pankaj's home?
qa.a: Screen time ends at eight.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj winding up to cry again?
qa.a: Crying had made Mummy give in yesterday, so Pankaj felt hopeful and determined to try it again.

qa.q: What did Minakshi change, and why does it help?
qa.a: She admitted giving in was unfair, kept the eight o'clock rule steady and offered a real choice, so Pankaj learns crying doesn't bend rules but fair choices exist.

qa.q: What is it like for Minakshi to stay calm while Pankaj wails?
qa.a: It is probably hard and tiring for Minakshi, but she stays firm because she sees that yesterday's giving in made bedtime harder.

grounding: Shows a child's bargaining growing when a parent gives in, and a parent restoring a fair, consistent limit.

passage: In their kitchen in Dublin, baby Tomas started howling in his bouncer while Mum was draining pasta. His big brother Daniel, five, looked up from his drawing. He ran to the toy basket, dug out the crinkly giraffe and waved it over the bouncer. "Look, Tomas! Giraffe!" Tomas hiccuped and grabbed its ear. Daniel patted his foot. Mum set down the pot. "Daniel, you saw Tomas was upset and brought him the giraffe. That really helped him calm down." Daniel stood a little taller. When Tomas fussed again after dinner, Daniel went straight for the giraffe.

qa.q: What toy did Daniel bring to Tomas?
qa.a: Daniel brought the crinkly giraffe.

qa.q: Why did Daniel stand a little taller after Mum spoke?
qa.a: Daniel felt proud because Mum praised exactly what he had done for Tomas.

qa.q: What made Mum's praise effective?
qa.a: Mum named the specific action, noticing Tomas was upset and bringing the giraffe, so Daniel knew what to repeat.

qa.q: How might baby Tomas experience his brother waving the giraffe?
qa.a: Tomas probably feels soothed and curious, grabbing the ear and settling down.

grounding: Illustrates a child fetching a toy for a crying baby brother, with the caring growing after specific praise.

passage: In the crowded waiting room of the health centre, baby Santosh screamed after his injection. Mummy rocked him, but he kept crying. His sister Seema, five, climbed off her chair, stroked his hand and sang the chanda mama song she knew he liked. His screams dropped to whimpers. The nurse at the desk leaned over. "Seema, you sang to your brother and stroked his hand so gently. That helped him calm down." Seema beamed and sang it again, softer this time, until Santosh's eyes began to close.

qa.q: What song did Seema sing to Santosh?
qa.a: Seema sang the chanda mama song.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she climbed off her chair?
qa.a: Seema seemed worried about her crying brother and wanted to help him feel better.

qa.q: How did the nurse encourage Seema's caring?
qa.a: The nurse praised the exact things Seema did, singing and stroking gently, so she wanted to keep doing them.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Seema's help in the waiting room?
qa.a: Mummy likely feels grateful and relieved to have Seema's help while rocking the baby 🙂

grounding: Shows a child soothing a crying baby brother and the caring growing when an adult praises the specific action.

passage:
Note to Akash's parents from Teacher Rukmini, Thursday
Since baby Bhavna arrived, Akash has changed at school. Today he crawled under the table at story time, sucking his thumb, and said, "I'm a baby too. Babies get carried." When I didn't carry him, he kicked the chair. I sat beside him and said, "It's big news, having a new sister. You still matter so much." Then I made him our Fish Helper, and he fed the fish very carefully 🙂
Could you give him a small job with Bhavna at home, like choosing her socks, and some time just with him?

qa.q: What job did Teacher Rukmini give Akash?
qa.a: Teacher Rukmini made him the Fish Helper.

qa.q: Why did Akash crawl under the table and say he was a baby too?
qa.a: Akash likely felt jealous and left out since baby Bhavna arrived, wishing to be cared for the way the baby is.

qa.q: What could Akash's parents try at home?
qa.a: Give Akash a special job with Bhavna, like choosing her socks, plus some time just with him, instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Akash's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They might feel worried or a bit guilty, but also grateful for a clear idea to help Akash.

grounding: Illustrates a child acting like a baby after a newborn sister arrives, and reassurance plus a special role instead of scolding.

passage: In their house near the backwaters, Amma sat on the mat feeding his baby sister Arohi. Jomon, five, threw his ball against the wall, again and again. "Jomon, stop that!" Appa called from the yard. Jomon threw himself down. "I want milk too! I'm a baby!" Amma didn't scold. She shifted Arohi and made room on her lap. "Come here, my big boy. I missed you today." Jomon curled against her. "Arohi likes your voice best," Amma said. "Will you sing her the boat song?" Jomon sniffed, then sang, loud and proud, while Arohi's tiny fingers opened and closed.

qa.q: What song did Amma ask Jomon to sing?
qa.a: Amma asked him to sing the boat song.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he threw his ball against the wall?
qa.a: Jomon felt jealous and left out while Amma fed baby Arohi, and wanted attention too.

qa.q: Which choice by Amma worked, and why?
qa.a: Instead of scolding, Amma made room on her lap and gave Jomon a special job singing to Arohi, so he felt loved and important.

qa.q: How might Appa see Jomon's outburst from the yard?
qa.a: Appa may first see it as naughtiness, though it is really Jomon's way of asking for attention after the new baby.

grounding: Shows a child acting out and wanting to be a baby while the mother feeds a newborn, eased by reassurance and a special role.

passage: At Disha's birthday party in the society community hall, Eshaan Mama handed her a soft parcel. She tore it open: a green sweater with a duck on it. Disha had wished for a doctor set. Her face fell for a second. Mummy caught her eye and gave a small nod. Disha looked at the sweater again. "Thank you, Eshaan Mama. The duck is funny." He laughed. "I picked it because you love ducks." That night at home, Disha whispered to Mummy, "I wanted a doctor set." Mummy hugged her. "I know. You were kind to Mama. We can talk about wishes any time."

qa.q: What was on the sweater Eshaan Mama gave Disha?
qa.a: The sweater had a duck on it.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when her face fell?
qa.a: Disha felt disappointed because she had wished for a doctor set, not a sweater.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Disha to wait until night to tell Mummy?
qa.a: Saying thank you at the party honoured Mama's kind intention, and telling Mummy privately let Disha be honest without hurting him.

qa.q: How does Eshaan Mama see Disha's thank-you?
qa.a: Eshaan Mama feels pleased that his thoughtful choice, picked because she loves ducks, was welcomed 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child thanking a relative for an unwanted gift, seeing his kind intention, and saving honesty for a private moment.

passage: I'm Kiran, Eshaan's cousin, and I saw his face when Nani gave him her present at Diwali. It was a thick rhyme book, not the toy car he'd talked about all week. His mouth went tight and he looked at the floor. I thought he might cry. Then he hugged the book and said, "Thank you, Nani." Nani smiled. "Your mummy loved these rhymes when she was small." Later, behind the curtain, I heard him tell his mummy softly, "I wanted the car." She nodded and said they could read one rhyme with Nani tomorrow. I still don't know how much he minded.

qa.q: What present did Nani give Eshaan at Diwali?
qa.a: Nani gave Eshaan a thick rhyme book.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's tight mouth suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Eshaan felt disappointed not to get the toy car, though Kiran can't be sure how much he minded.

qa.q: What did Eshaan's mummy get right when he told her about the car?
qa.a: She listened privately and turned the book into something to share with Nani, so Eshaan's honesty was heard without hurting Nani.

qa.q: How might Nani see the gift and Eshaan's hug?
qa.a: Nani likely sees the rhyme book as a family treasure and feels warm and happy when Eshaan hugs it.

grounding: Shows a child thanking a grandparent for an unwanted gift and saying the honest wish later, in private.

passage: In the colony park in Hyderabad, a boy Seema didn't know was crying by the swings, and she only watched from the see-saw. A little later her best friend Akash tripped on the path and scraped his knee. Seema ran over at once. She sat right beside him on the ground and held his hand. "Does it hurt a lot?" Akash nodded, sobbing. "I'll get Aunty Rehana," Seema said, and raced to the bench where his mother sat. She came back holding Aunty's hand and stayed beside Akash while his knee was cleaned.

qa.q: Where did Akash scrape his knee?
qa.a: Akash tripped on the path and scraped his knee.

qa.q: Why did Seema run to Akash at once but only watch the other boy?
qa.a: Seema felt worried for Akash because he is her best friend; the crying boy was a stranger, so she felt less pulled to help.

qa.q: What did Seema try that helped Akash most?
qa.a: She sat beside him, held his hand, asked how he felt and fetched his mother, which is just what a hurt friend needs.

qa.q: How does Akash see Seema sitting with him?
qa.a: Akash probably feels comforted and less alone, knowing his best friend is right beside him.

grounding: Illustrates a child comforting a hurt close friend by sitting beside him and fetching an adult, more readily than for a stranger.

passage:
"Kunal, why are you crying?"
"My mummy didn't come for pickup. Everyone went home."
Gurpreet sat down on the step right next to him. "I'll wait with you. My papa's late too."
"What if she forgot me?"
"She won't forget. You're her best boy." Gurpreet patted his back. "Let's tell Ma'am."
"Will she be angry?"
"No. Come." Gurpreet took his hand. "Ma'am! Kunal is sad. His mummy isn't here."
"Thank you for bringing him, Gurpreet. Kunal, I'll phone your mummy right now. Sit with me, both of you."
Kunal wiped his nose on his sleeve and held on to Gurpreet's hand.

qa.q: Why was Kunal crying on the step?
qa.a: His mummy didn't come for pickup, and everyone went home.

qa.q: What was Kunal worried about?
qa.a: Kunal was scared that his mummy had forgotten him.

qa.q: Which choice by Gurpreet helped most, and why?
qa.a: Taking Kunal to Ma'am helped most, because an adult could phone his mummy, while sitting close kept him from feeling alone.

qa.q: How does Ma'am see Gurpreet bringing Kunal over?
qa.a: Ma'am sees it as a caring, sensible act and thanks Gurpreet, then acts at once by phoning Kunal's mummy.

grounding: Shows a child comforting a crying friend by sitting beside him and bringing him to the teacher.

passage: Every evening in their Istanbul flat, Babaanne rolled out her prayer rug by the window. Tonight Selin, four, dragged a bath towel next to it. When Babaanne raised her hands, Selin raised hers. When Babaanne bowed and pressed her forehead to the rug, Selin pressed hers to the towel and peeked sideways. She whispered sounds that were almost like Babaanne's words. The room felt very quiet, just the traffic far below. Afterwards Babaanne cupped Selin's face and smiled. "My little companion." Selin folded her towel exactly the way Babaanne folded the rug.

qa.q: What did Selin use instead of a prayer rug?
qa.a: Selin used a bath towel.

qa.q: What might Selin have felt during the quiet prayer?
qa.a: Selin probably felt wonder and closeness to Babaanne, copying her movements without yet knowing what the words mean.

qa.q: How could Babaanne help Selin keep feeling she belongs?
qa.a: Keep welcoming her beside the rug, as with "My little companion", and explain a little in simple words when Selin asks.

qa.q: How does Babaanne see Selin copying her?
qa.a: Babaanne likely feels touched and joyful to have Selin beside her at prayer 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a young child copying a grandparent's prayer and feeling awe and belonging before understanding its meaning.

passage: In the home corner of their Kolkata preschool, Arnab set a wooden block on the toy shelf and put a paper flower in front of it. He rang the little tin bell three times, folded his hands and swayed, murmuring, "Ma, Ma, Ma." Darshan watched. "What are you doing?" "Puja. Like Thakuma does for Ma Kali every evening." "Why?" Arnab thought hard. "I don't know. It's for Ma. Everyone goes quiet and the lamp smells nice." Darshan folded his hands too. Miss Priya smiled and let them finish before calling them for snack.

qa.q: How many times did Arnab ring the tin bell?
qa.a: Arnab rang it three times.

qa.q: What does Arnab's answer "I don't know. It's for Ma" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Arnab feels awe and belonging in Thakuma's evening puja, even though he doesn't yet understand its meaning.

qa.q: How did Miss Priya handle the pretend puja respectfully?
qa.a: She smiled and let them finish before snack, without mocking or questioning the family's faith.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Arnab's puja?
qa.a: Darshan seems curious and drawn in, folding his hands too to share the moment.

grounding: Shows a young child copying the family's evening puja at play, feeling awe and belonging without knowing its meaning.
